title: Structured Analysis · 1 — Describe the Work Before You Build It
description: Why most failed software is the wrong thing built well, the three parts of every real system, and the chain of ideas from clean code to clear analysis. Plain English, read in full, with commentary.

title: Structured Analysis · 2 — Breaking a System Down
description: Data and control, building a diagram from outside events, the box with four arrows that describes any job, and why jobs and objects cut the world in different directions. Plain English, read in full, with commentary.

title: Structured Analysis · 3 — Follow the Data
description: Top-down analysis, DeMarco's four tools, the context diagram, and the data dictionary that keeps a system's words consistent. Full text read, with commentary.

title: Structured Analysis · 4 — Data Flows, Structure Charts, and Good Modules
description: Data-flow diagrams, structure charts, and the two principles that outlasted every method: cohesion and coupling. Plus how all the pieces fit together. Full text read, with commentary.

title: Software Architecture · 1 — The Decisions You Can't Undo
description: What software architecture really is, the one-question test for spotting it, and the two laws every architect lives by. A plain-English version of the Wikipedia article, read in full, with commentary.

title: Software Architecture · 2 — The Hidden Forces That Shape a System
description: Why qualities, not features, decide a system's shape; how business goals turn into "ilities"; views, conceptual integrity, and Conway's Law. A plain-English version of the Wikipedia article, read in full, with commentary.

title: Software Architecture · 3 — Shapes, Styles, and Patterns
description: Monolith versus distributed, four classic styles, the circuit breaker, and a six-step cycle for cutting a system into right-sized parts. A plain-English version of the Wikipedia article, read in full, with commentary.

title: Software Architecture · 4 — Deciding, Remembering, and Fighting Decay
description: The four activities architects repeat, two traps that catch almost everyone, decision records, erosion and the two lost years, and fitness functions. A plain-English version of the Wikipedia article, read in full, with commentary.
